Every Date, Name and Open Question in Your Husband's Care, in One Place

A one-page inventory of what you've been told, by whom and when, and what you still don't have.

Download PDF

The discharge date is on a whiteboard, the rehab's number is on the back of an envelope, and the pharmacist's question is in a voicemail.

This page doesn't ask you to work out what any of it means. It asks where each thing is, what date is on it, and who has it.

What to collectWhere it isIts dateWho has it

The pharmacy's questions
Appointments already booked
Names and phone numbers of the people to call with questions
The family's lists of things to do, including the ones other people are keeping
Questions nobody has answered yet
Offers of help: who offered, and what

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

The dates, one per line

Every date anyone has mentioned, including the ones you aren't sure about. If you can't remember who gave it, leave that box empty. The first line is an example.

The dateWhat it's forWho gave itIn writing?

What's missing, and who will ask for it

Anything above with an empty box. Put a name beside it once that person has said they'll ask.

For example Nobody has the discharge date in writing. Our daughter will ask the discharge planner tomorrow.

How to use it

  • For anything you were told out loud, write who said it and the day they said it.
  • Don't copy a document onto this page or sum it up. Note where it is.
  • If two people have different versions of the same date, write both, with who gave each.
  • Keep this page with the papers, and take both along when you talk to anyone on it.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any record, date or instruction means, and it doesn't put anything in order. If something you've collected isn't clear, that's a question for the person who wrote it or said it.

Ready for the next step?

You know where each date, name and piece of paper is, and which ones you still don't have. The care interview puts them to use: it walks you through your husband's situation area by area and turns your answers into a Family Care Profile you can bring to any care conversation.

Where this comes from

The rows for written discharge instructions, appointments, and names and phone numbers follow what Medicare's discharge checklist tells patients and caregivers to ask for and keep. Writing down who told you something, and on what date, follows the Family Caregiver Alliance. The rest come from the Family Care Roadmap's working list for this step.

  1. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Your Discharge Planning Checklist (CMS Product No. 11376)
  2. Family Caregiver Alliance, Caregiving at Home: A Guide to Community Resources
